A1.justification: Both PDFs describe causal differential networks for perturbation-target prediction. All 22 pages of each version, including appendix text, equations, tables and figures, support comparison despite substantial revisions.

before.justification: V1 Sections 4.1–4.2 and Appendix D report original biological and synthetic experiments, including target-prediction results, ablations, runtimes and uncertainty estimates.

after.justification: V2 Sections 4.1–4.2 and Appendix E report original biological and synthetic results, including revised model evaluations, additional baselines and new ablations.

M1.justification: V1 freezes the causal featurizer and trains a single-layer differential network. V2 jointly trains both modules, introduces graph supervision alongside target prediction, adds node-level mean and variance features, and supports concatenation or subtraction of graph representations. Its differential networks use three or two layers, respectively.

E1.justification: The seven biological datasets, six drug cases, and seen/unseen cell-line settings are retained; trivial perturbations remain evaluated in the appendix. Synthetic coverage expands through sigmoid test mechanisms and soft-shift training interventions, alongside the existing linear/polynomial and hard/scale-intervention settings.

E2.justification: V2 adds DGE to the genetic and chemical comparisons and MB+CI to the synthetic comparisons. These introduce substantial statistical competitors missing from v1. Existing learned baselines remain, while the explicit RANDOM rows in v1 Table 2 disappear.

E3.justification: Candidate padding changes from random genes to genes with greatest log-fold change. V2 adds Spearman correlation, removes tabular R20, and replaces absolute-k recall with fraction-based recall. Synthetic training expands from approximately 4,000 hard-only datasets to 8,640 including soft interventions and switches to correlation features. Real finetuning changes batch size, learning rate and precision.

E4.justification: V2 adds synthetic-only versus finetuned comparisons, a node-statistics ablation, combined removal of pretraining and graph supervision, learning curves, and comparisons of training with versus without scale interventions. New correlation-difference case studies appear in Figures 6–7. V1’s CDN-MLP accuracy comparisons and marginal/global-feature ablation tables are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report standard deviations over five synthetic datasets and five rounds of cell subsampling using the same 80%-with-minimum-50 rule. V2’s reference to five seeds describes the retained subsampling procedure; it does not establish additional training runs or a new uncertainty estimator.

E6.justification: Reported nontrivial, seen-cell-line CDN ranks span 0.55–0.72 in v1 Table 2 and 0.92–0.98 in v2 Table 1, under revised models and settings rather than an isolated same-setting comparison. Numerous baseline, sigmoid and ablation results are added. V1’s six drug scores survive, rounded, as v2’s CDN (no μ) row; the new full-model drug results are mixed.

T1.justification: The intervention-capacity constructions and assumptions move from v1 Appendix A to v2 Appendix C with essentially unchanged mathematics. V2 Section 3.1 adds a limited computational-cost derivation: ordinary attention over graph edges costs O(N^4), whereas axial attention costs O(N^3).

C1.justification: The abstract’s methodological contribution changes from pretrained graph featurization followed by supervised classification to jointly trained graph and target prediction with statistical features. The introduction strengthens unseen-cell-line generalization from maintaining decent performance to minimal performance drop. V1’s separately claimed contribution of preparing seven benchmark datasets is omitted.

C2.justification: V1 briefly flags poor doxorubicin performance. V2 explains the mismatch between drug effects on proteins and measured mRNA, discusses undetected off-target effects, and explicitly frames chemical evaluation as a proof of concept. It also introduces interpretations of transferable perturbation characteristics, node-statistics failures on drugs, and potential overfitting to familiar intervention types.

D1.justification: V2 substantially expands architecture and training documentation, including edge embeddings, sparse/dense attention, validation selection, stopping criteria, hidden dimension, weight decay, CPU workers and training times. It also specifies a UT-IGSP commit and additional simulation details. Raw-data accession codes remain, but v1’s explicit source-code release promise is omitted.

R1.justification: V2 substantially broadens the perturbation-modeling and causal-discovery discussion, adding works such as CellOT, AttentionPert, GIM, Petersen et al. and Montagna et al. It explicitly positions CDN as a supervised counterpart to DCI’s difference-based reasoning and adds drug-target literature. Several earlier citations, including Chevalley et al. and Reisach et al., disappear.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and related-work narrative are extensively rewritten. The problem statement becomes a dedicated subsection, methods are reorganized, and appendices gain separate architecture and training sections. The standalone conclusion and reproducibility statement disappear, while an impact statement replaces the ethics statement.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one to two columns. Figure 2 is substantially redrawn; recall plots expand from two K562 panels to five datasets with normalized axes. Tables are restructured, trivial results move to the appendix, and new heatmaps and training curves appear. Existing dataset-statistics plots are merged and relocated.

improvement.justification: Adding DGE resolves an important benchmarking weakness: it surpasses v1’s learned comparators, while v2’s revised CDN still exceeds it on genetic data. Intervention-type controls, fuller implementation details and explicit chemical limitations substantially strengthen evaluation and interpretability. These gains outweigh the removal of some earlier ablations, although the abstract’s seven-dataset superiority claim remains broader than the mixed chemical results support.
